title: 4 Weird Things Your Body Does (And Why Science Still Argues)

lines.text: Your body does four strange things every single day, and science still argues about why.
A yawn you can't stop. A hiccup out of nowhere. A sneeze from sunlight. A foot that falls asleep.
Let's take them one by one, starting with the one that's probably about to happen to you.
Number one: the yawn.
You do it when you're tired, when you're bored, or when you just watched someone else do it.
For years, people said you yawn to get more oxygen into your blood.
But old experiments found that breathing pure oxygen didn't reduce yawning, and extra carbon dioxide didn't increase it.
The leading idea today is that a yawn helps cool your brain.
In rats, brain temperature rose before a yawn, and dropped right after.
In one small human study, people told to breathe through their noses didn't catch yawns from others at all.
It's still not proven. Babies yawn in the womb, and so do cold-blooded animals, which is hard to explain with cooling.
And contagious yawning seems to be about connection, but only around six or seven in ten people catch it.
Number two: the hiccup.
A hiccup is a tiny glitch in your breathing.
Your diaphragm, the big muscle under your lungs, suddenly jerks downward, and you start to breathe in.
A split second later, your vocal cords snap shut. That snap is the hic sound.
The signal runs along two big nerves, the phrenic nerve and the vagus nerve.
But why do we do it? Nobody knows for sure.
One theory says it's a leftover from ancestors who breathed with gills. The control center for hiccups sits near the one that runs gill breathing in lower animals.
Another idea says it helped babies feed, like a burp. A third says it's breathing practice before birth.
Experts don't even agree on whether it helps us at all.
Number three: the sun sneeze.
Step out into bright light, and for some people, a sneeze comes out of nowhere.
It's called the photic sneeze reflex, and studies estimate somewhere between eighteen and thirty-five percent of people have it.
It runs in families. If one of your parents has it, you have about a fifty percent chance of having it too.
Scientists still don't know exactly how light sets it off.
The best guess is that signals from the eye cross over into nearby nerve pathways that also serve your nose.
It may be the sudden change in brightness that matters, more than the light itself.
It's harmless, with one catch: you close your eyes when you sneeze, which is a problem if you're driving.
Number four: the foot that falls asleep.
You sit on your foot for a while, and when you stand up, it buzzes like static.
The popular story says your foot ran out of blood.
But many scientists say the main cause is pressure on a nerve.
The nerve that serves your foot gets squeezed, so its messages can't get through, and the foot goes numb.
When you move and the pressure lifts, the nerve restarts, and its fibers fire in a scrambled way. That's the pins and needles.
It's harmless when it fades quickly. If it keeps coming back, get it checked.
Four strange habits of your body, and for every one of them, the full story is still being worked out.
